lesson.text: Genes are instructions carried on chromosomes inside cells. They help decide traits like eye colour, hair type and height.
Young get genes from their parents. In sexual reproduction, half come from each parent, so young are like their parents but not identical.
Different versions of a gene are called alleles. Some are dominant (they show when present); others are recessive (they show only if both copies are recessive).
In asexual reproduction, one parent makes young with the same genes: a strawberry runner makes a copy of the plant.

exercises.prompt: In sexual reproduction, where do a baby's genes come from?
Young from sexual reproduction are identical to one parent.
exercises.explain: No: they get a mix from both parents.

exercises.prompt: What does a dominant allele do?
exercises.explain: It shows whenever it is present.

exercises.prompt: When does a recessive trait show?
choices: only if both copies are recessive

exercises.prompt: A strawberry plant grows a runner that becomes a new plant. What kind of reproduction is it?
Brothers and sisters can look different because they get different mixes of their parents' genes.
Why are young from asexual reproduction like their parent?
Two brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child. How?
choices: Both carried a hidden recessive blue allele.
exercises.explain: Each parent passed on a hidden recessive allele.

exercises.prompt: Why can sexual reproduction help a species survive change?
exercises.explain: Varied young mean some may cope with new conditions.

exercises.prompt: Traits can be affected by both genes and the environment.
exercises.explain: Yes: food can affect how tall you grow.

exercises.hint: Genes are on chromosomes, inside cells.
